hook.situation: Explaining a choice that has both good and bad sides, or continuing with a plan despite a problem.
objectives: Use A/V-지만 for clean contrast: 비싸지만 맛있어요.
Use A/V-(으)ㄴ/는데도 when the result is surprising despite the situation: 비가 오는데도 사람이 많아요.
Use V아/어도 when the result stays the same even if the condition happens: 비가 와도 갈 거예요.
hook.whyItMatters: Learners often connect everything with 그리고 or translate every 'but' the same way. Korean separates simple contrast, surprising concession, and 'even if' conditions. This lets plans sound more precise and less flat.

grammarNotes.title: A/V-지만 — but
grammarNotes.func: Use -지만 to join two clauses that go against each other, like English "but." The first clause says one thing, and the second says something that pushes the other way.

formTable.when: Verb or adjective stem (consonant or vowel)
formTable.ex: 먹다 → 먹지만, 비싸다 → 비싸지만, 가다 → 가지만
먹다 → 먹었지만, 가다 → 갔지만, 공부하다 → 공부했지만

examples.en: This book is fun, but it's too long.
examples.note: 재미있- takes -지만 right on the stem; both clauses are about the same book.

examples.en: Korean is hard, but it's fun.
examples.note: The classic shape: one downside, then one upside.

examples.en: I ate, but I'm still hungry.
examples.note: Put the past tense on the first clause: 먹었- + 지만.

examples.en: My friend is a student, but works too.
examples.note: After a noun ending in a consonant, use 이지만: 학생 + 이지만.

keyPoint.label: -지만 vs. 하지만
keyPoint.body: -지만 connects two clauses inside one sentence: 비싸지만 맛있어요. 하지만 is a separate word that starts a new sentence: 비싸요. 하지만 맛있어요. Same meaning, but don't drop 하지만 in the middle of a clause — that spot belongs to -지만.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: After a final ㄱ or ㅈ-type sound the next syllable tightens: 먹지만 sounds like [먹찌만], 좋지만 like [조치만]. The 지만 part is never the loud part of the word.

drill.instruction: Join the two ideas into one sentence with A/V-지만. Keep any past tense on the first clause.
drill.model: 비싸다 / 사고 싶어요 → 비싸지만 사고 싶어요. (It's expensive, but I want to buy it.)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: -지만 goes on the plain stem (어렵-), not on the polite -아/어요 form. Drop the 요, attach -지만 to the stem, and let the politeness show up just once at the very end.

grammarNotes.title: A/V-(으)ㄴ/는데도 — even though, and still
grammarNotes.func: Use -(으)ㄴ/는데도 for "even though A, B anyway," where B is surprising given A. It points out that the result happened in spite of the first clause.

formTable.when: Adjective stem ending in a vowel
Adjective stem ending in a consonant

examples.en: Even though I took medicine, I'm still sick.
examples.note: 먹었- + 는데도; the second clause is the surprising part.

examples.en: Even though this restaurant is expensive, it's packed.
Even though I study every day, Korean is hard.
examples.note: Present verb 공부하- takes -는데도, the normal verb shape.

examples.en: Even though he has a lot of money, he barely spends it.

keyPoint.label: -(으)ㄴ/는데도 vs. -지만
keyPoint.body: -지만 is a flat "but." -(으)ㄴ/는데도 adds "and still," with a sense of surprise that B happened anyway. 약을 먹었지만 아파요 just states two facts; 약을 먹었는데도 아파요 sounds more like "I took the medicine and I'm STILL sick."

grammarNotes.pronunciation: Past forms nasalize: 먹었는데도 sounds like [머건는데도], 했는데도 like [핸는데도] — the ㅅ turns into an ㄴ sound before 는. The 도 at the end gets a small push for the "and still" feeling.

drill.instruction: Combine the two clauses with A/V-(으)ㄴ/는데도 for "even though A, B anyway." Watch verb vs. adjective endings.
drill.model: 운동하다 / 살이 안 빠져요 → 운동하는데도 살이 안 빠져요. (Even though I work out, I don't lose weight.)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners stick -는데도 on everything, but -는데도 is for verbs only. Adjectives take -(으)ㄴ데도: 비싸다 → 비싼데도, 좋다 → 좋은데도. Ask if the word is an action (verb → 는데도) or a description (adjective → ㄴ/은데도).

grammarNotes.title: V-아/어도 — even if / even though
grammarNotes.func: Use -아/어도 for "even if" or "even though." It means that no matter how the first clause turns out, the second clause still holds.

formTable.when: Stem with ㅏ or ㅗ as the last vowel
formTable.ex: 가다 → 가도, 오다 → 와도, 보다 → 봐도
먹다 → 먹어도, 읽다 → 읽어도, 마시다 → 마셔도

examples.en: Even if it rains, I go to school.
examples.note: 오다 → 와도; the going happens no matter the rain.

examples.en: No matter how much I eat, I don't get full.
examples.note: 아무리 ... -아/어도 is the set "no matter how much" frame.

examples.en: Even when I'm tired, I work out.
Even when I have no time, I still eat.
examples.note: 없- + 어도 → 없어도; the first clause is the condition you push through.

keyPoint.label: -아/어도 vs. -(으)ㄴ/는데도
keyPoint.body: Both can come out as "even though" in English, but -아/어도 covers "even IF" — it works for things that may or may not happen (비가 와도 = even if it rains, real or not). -(으)ㄴ/는데도 is for a real fact happening right now (비가 오는데도 = even though it IS raining). Use -아/어도 for conditions, -는데도 for facts.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: Watch the vowel squeeze: 오다 → 와도, 보다 → 봐도, 마시다 → 마셔도. The 도 stays quiet; the squeezed syllable carries the beat.

drill.instruction: Make a sentence with V-아/어도 for "even if / even though." Pick the right 아/어 vowel.
drill.model: 바쁘다 / 친구를 만나요 → 바빠도 친구를 만나요. (Even if I'm busy, I meet my friend.)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: There's no 서 in this pattern — -아/어도 attaches straight to the 아/어 stem. And don't mix it up with -아/어서 ("because"): -아/어서 gives a reason, while -아/어도 gives a concession ("even if").

exampleSentence.en: It is good. But it is a little expensive.
It is delicious. However, it is expensive.
exampleSentence.note: Use at the start of a new sentence.

exampleSentence.en: It is a little inconvenient. However, it is possible.
exampleSentence.note: A slightly fuller form of 하지만.

exampleSentence.en: It is expensive. Even so, shall we try going?
exampleSentence.note: 그래도 keeps the plan or feeling despite the previous sentence.
A core contrast adjective for shopping and restaurants.

exampleSentence.en: It is cheap, but the quality is good.
Even if it is easy, you can make a mistake.
I will continue even if I am tired.
I will keep going even if it is hard.
It is okay even if there is a problem.
There are drawbacks too, but there are more advantages.
Even if there is a drawback, I am okay with it.
It is okay even if it is a little inconvenient.
It is a little inconvenient, but possible.
It does not matter even if it is expensive.

extendedDialogue.setting: Friends decide whether to go to a popular restaurant despite price, crowds, and rain.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: This restaurant is expensive, but really delicious.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: But there are too many people today.
lines.grammarNote: 그런데 softens the turn into a concern.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Even if there are many people, the food comes out quickly.
lines.grammarNote: -아/어도 keeps the result despite the condition.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.en: Even though it is raining, there are many people waiting.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Even so, shall we try going?
lines.grammarNote: 그래도 keeps the plan alive despite the problem.

readingText.title: A good plan with drawbacks
readingText.body: 민서는 새 식당에 가 보고 싶었어요. 그 식당은 비싸지만 음식이 맛있고 서비스도 좋다고 했어요. 지훈은 사람이 너무 많아서 걱정했지만, 민서는 사람이 많아도 음식이 빨리 나온다고 말했어요. 밖에는 비가 오는데도 기다리는 사람이 많았어요. 지훈은 조금 불편해도 괜찮다고 했고, 두 사람은 그래도 한번 가 보기로 했어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Minseo wanted to try a new restaurant. It was expensive, but people said the food was good and the service was good. Jihoon worried because there were many people, but Minseo said the food comes out quickly even when it is crowded. Even though it was raining, many people were waiting. They decided to try going anyway.

culturalNote.title: Softening disagreement
culturalNote.body: In Korean conversation, contrast markers can soften disagreement. 그런데 introduces a concern gently, 하지만 is clearer and firmer, and 그래도 keeps a plan or feeling alive after acknowledging the problem.
culturalNote.tip: For a friendly disagreement, start with 맞아요 or 좋아요, then add 그런데: 좋아요. 그런데 조금 비싸요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence contrasts price and quality?
Which sentence keeps the plan despite rain?
inlineExercises.explanation: -아/어도 means even if or even though.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say 'Even though it is raining, there are many people.'
Fix the sentence: 비가 오아도 가요.
inlineExercises.explanation: 오다 contracts to 와 before 도.

inlineExercises.prompt: 비___ 와도 갈 거예요. (Even if it rains, I will go.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 비 is the subject of 오다, so it takes 가. 를 would make rain an object, which does not fit the weather verb 오다.
-지만 attaches directly to the stem for a clean contrast. 비싸다 becomes 비싸지만.
-지만 gives a simple but contrast. The sentence balances the negative point with the positive result.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'Even though I am tired, I keep studying.'
inlineExercises.explanation: -ㄴ데도 shows a surprising result despite the situation. 피곤한데도 keeps the contrast stronger than simple 피곤하지만.

inlineExercises.prompt: Fix the sentence: '어렵지만 할 수 없어요.' (intended: difficult but possible)
inlineExercises.explanation: The intended meaning is that it is possible, so use 할 수 있어요. 할 수 없어요 says the opposite: cannot do it.

bullets: -는데도 adds surprise or frustration: 비가 오는데도 사람이 많아요.
-아/어도 keeps the result despite the condition: 비가 와도 갈 거예요.
그런데, 하지만, and 그래도 differ in tone: soft concern, clear contrast, and even-so continuation.

writingTask.prompt: Write 3 sentences about something you bought or studied, noting one drawback that didn't stop you.
writingTask.hint: Use A/V-지만 for 'but' (비싸지만), A/V-(으)ㄴ/는데도 for 'even though' (어려운데도), and V-아/어도 for 'even if' (피곤해도).
writingTask.model: 이 가방은 비싸지만 정말 마음에 들어요. 한국어가 어려운데도 계속 공부해요. 피곤해도 매일 연습할 거예요.
writingTask.modelEn: This bag is expensive but I really like it. Even though Korean is hard, I keep studying. Even if I'm tired, I'll practice every day.

canDo: Join two opposing ideas with A/V-지만 (비싸지만 좋아요)
Say something happened in spite of A with A/V-(으)ㄴ/는데도 (어려운데도 공부해요)
Say a result holds no matter what with V-아/어도 (피곤해도 가요)
